en: Cariyāpiṭaka, Yudhañjayavagga, Saccapāramī 4: The Perfection of Truth 4. Once upon a time, O monks, the Bodhisatta was born as a king named Yudhañjaya, the son of King Mahāpatāpa. He was wise, intelligent, and possessed of great power. He ruled his kingdom righteously, and his subjects lived in peace and prosperity. Now, at that time, there was a certain brahmin who had made a vow to offer a sacrifice to the gods. He required the heart and blood of a man who had never told a lie in his life. Having heard of King Yudhañjaya’s reputation for truthfulness, he went to the palace and requested the king to grant him such a person. The king replied, "I am a man who has always spoken the truth; there is no one else who knows me better than I do. The brahmin said, "If you yourself are such a man, then give me your own heart and blood. The king thought to himself, "If I refuse this man, he will surely go elsewhere and cause harm to many people. It is better that I sacrifice my own life for the sake of others. With a mind full of compassion, he consented. He summoned a skilled surgeon and instructed him to take his heart and blood. As the surgery was being performed, the king remained calm and composed, recollecting the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Sangha. He spoke these words of truth: "By the power of this truth— That I have never uttered a falsehood, Even in jest or in play— May my body remain unharmed! As soon as he spoke these words, by the power of his truth, his body became whole again, just as it was before. The surgeon, seeing this miracle, was filled with wonder and reported it to the king. The king then gave the brahmin his heart and blood, saying, "Take them and fulfill your purpose. Having received them, the brahmin completed his sacrifice. The king, having fulfilled his promise, passed away and was reborn in a heavenly realm. Thus, monks, through the power of truth, the Bodhisatta sacrificed his own life for the sake of others. This, monks, is the perfection of truth (saccapāramī) practiced by the Bodhisatta in a former life.
The Conduct of the King of Crabs: "Furthermore,
when I was the king of crabs in a great lake..."
Under the heat of the sun,
the water in the lake dried up;
then crows and vultures [descended].
The herons, hawks, and falcons sit waiting for fish and devour them day and night.
Thus I thought there,
oppressed along with my kinsmen:
"By what means indeed..."
"May I deliver my kinsmen from suffering.
Having reflected upon the goal of the Dhamma,
he saw truth as his refuge.
Standing firm in truth,
I liberated my kinsmen from that great suffering by recollecting the Dhamma of the virtuous.
Reflecting upon the ultimate truth,
I performed an act of truth regarding whatever in the world is permanent and eternal.
"As far back as I can remember,
since I have attained the state of discernment,
I do not recall intentionally—
Not even a single living being has been harmed.
By this declaration of truth,
may Pajjunna send down rain!
Threaten Pajjuna,
destroy the treasure of the crow;
subject the crow to grief.
"Release the fish from their sorrows!
As soon as this true boon was uttered,
Pajjunna thundered forth.
Filling the plains and the valleys,
you rain down in an instant.
Such is this supreme truth:
Having exerted supreme effort,
I caused a great cloud to rain,
relying on the power of the majesty of my truth.
“There is none equal to me in truth;
this is my perfection of truth.
Thus ends the tenth practice, the Conduct of Maccharāja.
